title: Feet toward the Kaaba
hook: tradition says that at Mecca, told his feet pointed at God's house, he asked them to turn his feet where God is not

segments.voice: Yesterday, water to the west at Hardwar. Your line was why do we do this. Which habit did you ask, and did it have a good answer? Day thirty-seven.

Yesterday Nanak stood in the Ganges. Today, tradition takes him about as far west as his journeys go: to Mecca, the holiest city of Islam, where the Kaaba stands, the house Muslims face when they pray, from every corner of the earth. Picture a long day of travel. A tired man in a traveler's clothes lies down to sleep in the courtyard, and without thinking about it, stretches out with his feet pointing toward the Kaaba. In the morning a qazi, a religious judge, finds him there. And he's upset, for a reason anyone can understand: to point your feet at something is, in that culture and many others, a sign of disrespect. Today, what Nanak said back.
screen: `AS FAR WEST AS THE JOURNEYS GO.` → `A TRAVELER ASLEEP AT MECCA.` → `HIS FEET POINT AT THE KAABA.`

segments.voice: The qazi shakes him awake. How dare you point your feet at the house of God? And Nanak, tradition says, answers without any anger at all. Then please, turn my feet toward the direction where God is not. That's the whole story, in its oldest telling. Bhai Gurdas, a Sikh poet who wrote it down within a century or so of Nanak's life, tells it in his verses. Later tellings add a wonder: when the qazi dragged Nanak's feet around, the Kaaba seemed to turn with them. Whether it's a miracle or a picture, the question is the heart of it. Which way is God not? Here's the thing that makes this story generous rather than rude. The qazi's own tradition already agrees with the answer. Muslims face the Kaaba to pray as one community, in one direction; they don't say God lives inside a building. The Qur'an itself says that the east and the west both belong to God, and that wherever you turn, there is the face of God. So the story isn't a Sikh scoring a point off Islam. Sikhs tell it as Nanak reminding a pious man of something his own faith already held, the way a friend might remind you of your own best idea. And for Sikhs it echoes the very first symbol of their scripture. If there is one, and the one is in everything, then there is no direction to point your feet that's empty of God. Not east, not west, not down. Every direction is full.
screen: `TURN MY FEET WHERE GOD IS NOT.` · `BHAI GURDAS TELLS IT IN HIS VERSES.` · `WHEREVER YOU TURN, THE FACE OF GOD.` · `EVERY DIRECTION IS FULL.` · then, large: `WHICH WAY IS GOD NOT?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: face four directions, slowly. Stand up if you can. Face one way, take a breath, and just notice what's in front of you, even if it's a wall. Then turn a quarter, and breathe again. Then another quarter. Then the last. If you believe in God, you can ask with each turn: is God here too? If you don't, notice that every direction has something in it worth seeing. The bell holds the time.
Feet toward the Kaaba. Guru Nanak at Mecca, asked to turn his feet away from God's house, asking which way God is not. Today's word.
Your line: which way is god not. Today, in the least holy-looking place you visit, the parking lot, the laundry room, ask it once. Day thirty-seven.

screen: `DAY 37 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE HAND ON THE ROCK.`

howItsDone: Sikhs tell the Mecca sakhi, recorded by Bhai Gurdas in his first Var, as a teaching that God is present in every direction; it is often told alongside the Hardwar story as a pair.

fork.setup: you're a tired traveler in Mecca. a judge wakes you, angry that your feet point at the house of God. what do you say?
options: ask him to turn your feet where God is not.
argue that the building is only stone.
fork.reveal: tradition says Nanak asked him, calmly, to turn his feet toward wherever God is not. there was no such direction.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about bad manners at a holy place.
what it means: God isn't in one direction; every direction is full.
what a scholar hears: Bhai Gurdas's first Var tells it; the turning Kaaba is a later addition; and the Qur'an's own line, wherever you turn is the face of God, stands behind the qazi too.
